content: West Nile virus is primarily transmitted to humans through the bite of an infected mosquito. However, in rare cases, the virus can also be spread through blood transfusion, organ transplantation, or from a mother to her baby during pregnancy, childbirth, or breastfeeding. Most individuals infected with West Nile virus do not experience any symptoms. For those who do, symptoms may include fever, headache, fatigue, nausea, vomiting, muscle aches, and sometimes a rash. These symptoms typically last from a few days to a few weeks. However, some individuals may develop more severe forms of the disease. People over the age of 60 and those with certain underlying medical conditions are at a higher risk of developing serious illness. Severe symptoms of West Nile virus infection can include high fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, disorientation, coma, tremors, seizures, muscle weakness, vision loss, numbness, and paralysis. West Nile virus is found in many countries worldwide. Travelers visiting regions such as Africa, Europe, the Middle East, western and central Asia, or North America may be at risk of contracting the virus. Activities that increase exposure to mosquitoes, such as spending extended periods outdoors or traveling during mosquito-heavy seasons like summer, can elevate the risk of infection. Currently, there are no vaccines or specific medications available to prevent West Nile virus infection. Travelers can protect themselves by taking measures to avoid mosquito bites. Using EPA-registered insect repellents containing active ingredients such as DEET, picaridin, IR3535, or oil of lemon eucalyptus (OLE) is recommended. These repellents are safe and effective when used as directed, even for pregnant and breastfeeding women. If using sunscreen, apply insect repellent after applying sunscreen. For infants and children, additional precautions should be taken. Dress them in clothing that covers their arms and legs, and use mosquito netting over strollers and baby carriers. When applying insect repellent to children, follow label instructions carefully. Avoid using products containing OLE or para-menthane-diol (PMD) on children under three years old. Do not apply repellent to a child’s hands, eyes, mouth, or irritated skin. Adults should spray repellent onto their hands first and then apply it to a child’s face. Permethrin-treated clothing and gear, such as boots, pants, socks, and tents, can provide additional protection. Permethrin is an insecticide that kills or repels mosquitoes and other insects. Treated clothing remains effective after multiple washes, but it is important to follow product instructions for proper use. Permethrin products should not be applied directly to the skin. To keep mosquitoes out of your accommodations, choose lodging with air conditioning or screened windows and doors. If staying in a place without these features or sleeping outdoors, use a mosquito net. Opt for a compact, white, rectangular mosquito net with 156 holes per square inch, long enough to tuck under the mattress. Permethrin-treated mosquito nets offer enhanced protection compared to untreated ones. Follow label instructions to determine if treated nets can be washed. If bitten by mosquitoes, avoid scratching the bites. Apply over-the-counter anti-itch or antihistamine creams to relieve itching. For more information on mosquito bite symptoms and treatment, consult reliable health resources.
